newsitem.title: CANADA: FEATURE - Canada tax cuts becoming political issue.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Canada tax cuts becoming political issue.

text.p: With the U.S. presidential election campaign focusing on tax cuts, Canada's ruling Liberal Party, facing an election itself next year, is coming under pressure to reward heavily taxed Canadians with some relief of their own.

Liberal Finance Minister Paul Martin has to deal with a vocal lobby even inside his own party to provide some relief to citizens groaning under a system where the top individual income tax rate in some provinces is just below 55 percent.
Steep provincial and federal sales taxes add to the burden of hard-pressed consumers.
After two years of fiscal austerity concentrating on reducing provincial deficits, economists are adding to the clamour for tax relief.

Many argue that recent reductions in domestic interest rates are not enough to kick-start Canada's sluggish economy and that taxes must be lowered before cash-strapped Canadians will increase spending and spur any economic recovery.
On the political front, a federal election is likely next year and opposition parties are eyeing tax cuts as a major platform from which to launch an attack on the government.

The Conservatives, who lost power in 1993 and have since shrunk to just two seats in the 295-seat House of Commons, vowed at a party convention last month to push for a 10-20 percent income tax reduction in their first term of office -- if by some remote chance they manage to be re-elected.
Preston Manning, leader of the populist Reform Party has also hinted that he will have have the promise of a tax cut up his sleeve when election time rolls around.
"If he likes my haircut, wait till he sees my tax cut," Manning told reporters last week after Prime Minister Jean Chretien joked in parliament about his new hairdo.

Martin has so far remained committed to his tough deficit-reduction targets and has stated repeatedly that Canada cannot afford a tax cut while its fiscal affairs remain a mess. So far, he has the support of his government and many of the country's leading economists.

"For a country with a public sector debt to gross domestic product (GDP) ratio of 115 percent to talk about a tax cut in this environment is way premature," said David Rosenberg, senior economist at Nesbitt Burns. "For people to talk about tax cuts in this environment is irresponsible."
REDUCING FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL DEBT MUST BE THE PRIORITY

Rosenberg said reducing Canada's federal deficit, which is forecast to drop to C$24.3 billion (US$17.7 billion) in fiscal 1996/97, and its huge federal and provincial debt, which exceeds C$900 billion (US$657 billion), must remain the primary objective of fiscal policy.
He discarded one of the main arguments of the would-be tax cutters, who believe lower interest rates alone are insufficient to revive consumer demand.

"The problem is that fiscal drag impacts the economy on day one," Rosenberg said. "Monetary policy influences the economy with a much longer time lag. But make no mistake that this environment right now is going to do its job in reviving the economy."
The Bank of Canada has cut interest rates by four percentage points since last May in an effort to jump-start the economy and boost moribund domestic demand.
But for Canadians, whose debt-to-income ratio is at a record 94 percent, lower interest rates have largely meant an easier way to pay off debt, not an invitation to spend more.

"Interest rate relief is good, but if (consumers) don't have the money in their pocket to spend it, you're not going to see a boom in retail and big spending," said Steve Saldanha, economic analyst with Canada Trust.
"A tax cut right now could do wonders for the economy," Saldanha said.
He noted the government was on track to meet, and possibly exceed, its deficit targets due to its prudent economic assumptions, lower interest rates and unused contingency reserves.
EXCESS CASH RESERVES COULD FINANCE MODERATE TAX CUT
This excess cash could be used to finance a moderate tax cut without jeopardising Martin's deficit targets, Saldanha said.

Avery Shenfeld, senior economist at CIBC/Wood Gundy, agreed. "The interest cost savings that the federal government is likely to see over the next two years will be able to fund a reasonably sized tax cut without putting the targets in jeopardy," he said.
Citing examples of successful tax cutting policies in the United States, Shenfeld believes Canada's goverment would also score telling political points if it opted to cut taxes.

"I think politically tax cuts are proving to be the popular way to go," Shenfeld said. "Politicians in Canada are looking at the lessons of (Ontario Premier) Mike Harris and (Governor) Christine Whitman of New Jersey in realising that the public is getting fatigued with deficit reduction and would like to see some rewards for that."
Harris won the leadership of Canada's richest province last year by promising Ontarians a 30 percent income tax cut over five years and a balanced budget by the year 2000.

Martin, even though he has admitted that he will undershoot at least his 1995/96 (April-March) deficit target, has challenged anybody who proposes a tax cut to show clearly which areas of spending they will cut to compensate.

But analysts said he may give in to a modest tax cut in what will probably be his last budget before the federal election. Some said a cut in unemployment insurance premiums, in effect a corporate tax cut, would help create much needed jobs. The unemployment insurance fund has an estimated surplus between C$3.0 and C$5.0 billion (US$2.2 to US$3.65 billion) which economists said could be used to fund a cut in premiums.
Others said a modest personal income tax reduction could be a welcome shot in the arm of weak consumer demand.
But with the Liberal party enjoying an impressive lead in opinion polls, some said tax cuts may not be necessary to win the next election.
